quests.instruction: Which respelling matches a typical Southern British pronunciation?
quests.hint: Say both aloud and feel the jaw. One vowel is short and flat, like the one in 'cat'. The other is long and open, like the one in 'father'.
quests.explanation: Many Southern British speakers use the long open vowel /ɑː/ in can't. Most General American speakers use the short /æ/ from 'cat'. Same word, different vowel.
quests.dialectNote: Northern English speakers often use the short vowel too, so 'British' is not one single sound here.

quests.instruction: Pick the version you would expect from many General American speakers.
quests.hint: Compare the vowel with the one in 'father'. In which version does your mouth open wider and the vowel last longer?
quests.explanation: The vowel in dance is the short /æ/ of 'cat' for most American speakers. Southern British models stretch it to /ɑː/ before the 'ns' ending.
quests.dialectNote: The lengthening depends on the following consonants. 'Cat' and 'dad' keep their short vowel in both varieties.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits a Southern British accent?
quests.hint: Stress lands on the same syllable in both versions, so ignore stress. Only the vowel inside that syllable differs.
quests.explanation: The stressed vowel follows the same split as dance: /ɑː/ in many Southern British accents, /æ/ in General American.
quests.dialectNote: Listen to the stressed syllable rather than the spelling. The letter 'a' here does not decide the sound.

quests.instruction: Which version matches typical General American speech?
quests.hint: One vowel is rounded, with the lips pushed forward slightly. The other is unrounded and more relaxed, like a 'ah' you would say at the doctor's.
quests.explanation: In hot, many American speakers use an unrounded /ɑ/. Many Southern British speakers keep a short rounded /ɒ/.
quests.dialectNote: This vowel is one of the most reliable differences between the two big reference accents, though not every speaker follows it.

quests.instruction: Which respelling is closer to a Southern British pronunciation?
quests.hint: Look at your lips. In one version they round a little; in the other your jaw drops and the lips stay neutral.
quests.explanation: The short rounded /ɒ/ is characteristic of Southern British English. General American speakers typically say /ɑ/ here.
quests.dialectNote: Spelling gives no clue. The letter 'o' is pronounced differently in the two systems, so listen for lip rounding.

quests.instruction: Which form would you expect more often from an American speaker?
quests.hint: Focus on the first syllable only. The ending 'ing' is the same in both.
quests.explanation: The same lot vowel appears inside longer words. General American /ɑ/ gives 'SHAH-ping'; Southern British /ɒ/ gives a rounder 'SHOP-ing'.
quests.dialectNote: A vowel pattern travels with the word family: shop, stop, box and job all shift the same way.

quests.instruction: Which version reflects a non-rhotic accent such as Southern British English?
quests.hint: Ask whether the tongue curls back at the end of the word. One version finishes with an 'r' colour, the other simply ends on the vowel.
quests.explanation: Non-rhotic accents do not pronounce /r/ after a vowel at the end of a word, so car ends on 'ah'. Rhotic accents such as General American keep the /r/.
quests.dialectNote: Rhoticity is a system-wide pattern, not a property of one word. It affects hundreds of words.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of General American?
quests.hint: Listen to the very last sound. One ends with a curled or 'bunched' tongue; the other ends on a weak 'uh'.
quests.explanation: General American is rhotic, so the last syllable has an r-coloured vowel. Non-rhotic accents replace it with a weak /ə/.
quests.dialectNote: The last syllable is unstressed, but the rhotic pattern still applies. It appears in teacher, water and computer as well.

quests.instruction: Which respelling would fit many non-rhotic British speakers?
quests.hint: The 'r' sits in the middle of the word here, before a consonant. Ask whether it can be heard as a separate sound.
quests.explanation: Non-rhotic speakers drop /r/ before a consonant, leaving a long 'aw' vowel. Rhotic speakers keep it.
quests.dialectNote: Position matters. A non-rhotic accent can still say /r/ before a vowel, as in 'red' or 'very'.

quests.instruction: Which respelling matches typical General American speech?
quests.hint: The stress is the same. Look at the middle vowel: is it the vowel of 'day' or the vowel of 'spa'?
quests.explanation: American speakers say the middle vowel like 'day'. Many British speakers say it like 'spa', because it belongs to the long /ɑː/ group.
quests.dialectNote: Some words simply differ between dialects. You do not need a rule; you learn them as pairs.

quests.instruction: Which version is more usual in Southern British English?
quests.hint: Two things differ: the vowel and the final consonant. Focus on the vowel first.
quests.explanation: British English usually has /vɑːz/ with a long open vowel and a 'z'. American English uses /veɪs/, rhyming with 'face'.
quests.dialectNote: Both forms are understood everywhere. Some speakers also mix them, and you may hear /veɪz/ as well.

quests.instruction: Which respelling would fit General American?
quests.hint: Listen to how the word begins. One version starts like 'school', the other like 'shoe'.
quests.explanation: American English pronounces 'ch' in this word as /sk/. British English traditionally uses /ʃ/, as in 'shed'.
quests.dialectNote: The spelling 'sch' is pronounced differently in words like school and schedule, so spelling is unreliable.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of General American?
quests.hint: Look at the ending. One version ends with a weak syllable, the other with a syllable that sounds like 'file'.
quests.explanation: American English usually reduces the ending to a weak syllable. Southern British English often says it with a full /aɪl/.
quests.dialectNote: This suffix shows up in a whole group of words, not only one.

quests.instruction: Which respelling is more typical of British speech?
quests.hint: The first half of the word is identical. Compare only the ending.
quests.explanation: Many British speakers give the ending a full 'eye-l' sound in fragile. Most Americans reduce it to a weak vowel plus l.
quests.dialectNote: This is a tendency, not a law. Some speakers in each country use the other form.

quests.instruction: Which version fits General American?
quests.hint: This word combines two differences you have already met: the first vowel and the ending.
quests.explanation: In American English both changes happen together, giving an unrounded first vowel and a weak ending. British English keeps the rounded vowel and the full 'eye-l'.
quests.dialectNote: When two features combine, one of them may still be enough to tell the accents apart.

quests.instruction: Which respelling shows the American way of saying the middle consonant?
quests.hint: Listen to the middle of the word. One version has a crisp, released stop; the other is closer to a quick tap of the tongue.
quests.explanation: American speakers usually turn a /t/ between vowels into a quick voiced tap that sounds like /d/. A careful Southern British model keeps a clear /t/.
quests.dialectNote: The tap is common across North America and also in Australia and Ireland to different degrees.

quests.instruction: Which version matches a careful Southern British model?
quests.hint: Notice whether the middle sound is a crisp 't' or a soft, quick 'd'.
quests.explanation: The reference British model keeps a clear /t/. In everyday speech many British speakers use a glottal stop instead, while Americans often use the tap.
quests.dialectNote: Neither 't' nor a tap is more correct. They belong to different speech habits.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits American English?
quests.hint: Say the word quickly and notice what the tongue does in the middle: a full closure, or a light tap?
quests.explanation: The /t/ sits between two vowels, so many American speakers tap it. The result sounds like 'SID-ee'.
quests.dialectNote: You hear the tap in fast speech everywhere in the United States and Canada.

quests.instruction: Which respelling matches typical General American?
quests.hint: Listen to the moment after the 'n'. In one version there is a small 'y' glide before the vowel.
quests.explanation: In General American the /j/ glide is dropped after /n/, so news sounds like 'nooz'. Southern British keeps it: /njuːz/.
quests.dialectNote: This is called yod-dropping. It follows a consistent pattern after n, t, d and s.

quests.instruction: Which version is closer to Southern British?
quests.hint: Compare the sound just after 'st'. Is there a small 'y' glide before the vowel?
quests.explanation: Southern British speakers say /ˈstjuːdənt/ with the glide. General American usually says /ˈstuːdənt/.
quests.dialectNote: The glide is a different sound from the ‘ch’ that appears in some casual British forms of the word.

quests.instruction: Which respelling suits Southern British English?
quests.hint: The same glide is hiding inside a longer word. Listen for it in the final syllable.
quests.explanation: Southern British keeps /j/ in avenue: /ˈævənjuː/. American English drops it, giving /ˈævənuː/.
quests.dialectNote: The pattern still applies after an unstressed syllable. It is not limited to short words.

quests.instruction: Which respelling fits American English?
quests.hint: Ask yourself if the word starts with a breathy 'h' or directly with the vowel.
quests.explanation: American speakers usually leave out the /h/, so herb starts with the vowel. British speakers pronounce it.
quests.dialectNote: The spelling of herb has an 'h', but the American pronunciation is centuries old rather than a mistake.

quests.instruction: Which version is more typical of General American?
quests.hint: Compare only the first syllable. One rhymes with 'tea', the other with 'pet'.
quests.explanation: Many American speakers say the first vowel like 'ee', while British speakers say /ˈleʒə/ with the short vowel of 'pet'.
quests.dialectNote: American speakers vary, and the short-vowel form is also heard in the United States.

quests.instruction: Which version would many British speakers use?
quests.hint: Where does the stress fall? One version starts strong, the other has a weak first syllable.
quests.explanation: A common British form puts stress on the first syllable, /ˈɡærɪdʒ/. American English stresses the second, /ɡəˈrɑːʒ/.
quests.dialectNote: British speakers also use /ˈɡærɑːʒ/. Word origin from French explains why the stress moves.

quests.instruction: Which stress pattern is more usual in Southern British English?
quests.hint: Say both aloud. One version emphasises the beginning; the other pushes the end.
quests.explanation: British English tends to keep stress early in many French loan words: /ˈkæfeɪ/. American English often moves stress to the last syllable.
quests.dialectNote: French loans often show stress differences. You will meet more of them later.

quests.instruction: Which stress pattern would many Americans use?
quests.hint: Tap the rhythm on your desk. The stressed syllable is the loudest, longest one.
quests.explanation: American English usually stresses the first syllable in magazine. British English commonly stresses the last.
quests.dialectNote: Both patterns are understood in both countries; the difference is one of preference.

quests.instruction: Which version is more typical of British English?
quests.hint: Two things change: where the strong beat falls and how the syllable before 'ment' sounds.
quests.explanation: British English says /ədˈvɜːtɪsmənt/, with stress early and a weak 'is'. American English has a strong 'tize' syllable.
quests.dialectNote: Stress can change a word's shape so much that it sounds like a different word.

quests.instruction: Which version fits Southern British speech?
quests.hint: This word contains the same vowel contrast you met in dance and can't. Ask which one it belongs to.
quests.explanation: Bath takes the long /ɑː/ in Southern British English. General American keeps the short /æ/.
quests.dialectNote: The ‘th’ after the vowel is one of the contexts that triggers the long vowel in the south.

quests.instruction: Which respelling fits General American?
quests.hint: Two features are combined: the first vowel and the last syllable.
quests.explanation: General American uses unrounded /ɑ/ in the first syllable and an r-coloured ending. Non-rhotic Southern British says /ˈdɒktə/.
quests.dialectNote: Real speech often stacks several features. You can identify the accent from either one.

quests.instruction: Which version matches a non-rhotic British speaker?
quests.hint: Listen to two places: the vowel in the first syllable and the middle consonant.
quests.explanation: Non-rhotic speakers drop the /r/ and keep a clear /t/, giving /ˈpɑːti/. Americans keep /r/ and often tap the /t/.
quests.dialectNote: The two changes are independent, so a speaker could use one without the other.
